active_paradigms.idea: JIT-compile the existing deterministic hierarchy with torch.jit.script before changing placement quality
active_paradigms.description: The current program is a three-stage per-layer heuristic: descending-LPT packs fixed logical groups onto nodes, greedy water-filling creates copies independently inside each node, and another descending-LPT packs copies across that node's GPUs. Its principal strength is that every stage respects exact cardinalities and produces valid inverse maps, while the greedy replica rule is optimal for its simplified per-node equal-split model. Its main runtime weakness is Python-level iteration over layers, Python heaps, conversion through .tolist(), and reconstruction of tensors after packing. Preserve the exact algorithm and semantics, but express balanced_packing and replicate_experts in TorchScript-compatible tensor/control-flow form and compile the helper functions with torch.jit.script at module initialization. In particular, keep all intermediate tensors on CPU and eliminate Python list materialization so the evaluator sees identical placement decisions except for documented deterministic tie ordering. This is a deliberately low-risk first experiment because the supplied adapter exposes only combined_score, not the original evaluator's internal quality/time formula; if runtime contributes materially, it can improve score without sacrificing the already-working 0.129749 load behavior. Benchmark cold-import as well as repeated invocation, since evaluator timing may include compilation.
active_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Execution-time component of the combined score while retaining the current valid hierarchical load-balancing result exactly; use this as the safe baseline before quality-changing experiments.
active_paradigms.cautions: Do not invoke scripting inside rebalance_experts on every call, because compilation startup can overwhelm any gain. TorchScript has restrictions on nested functions, dynamic Python tuples, heapq, and some tensor APIs, so move helpers to module scope and replace heap/list state only where equivalence is verified. Preserve stable expert-ID tie breaking, int64 output dtype, CPU outputs, and the -1 padding convention in log2phy.

active_paradigms.idea: Use hierarchical agglomerative clustering to form load-affinity-aware node groups instead of treating consecutive expert IDs as the only group units
active_paradigms.description: The quality limitation in the current code is structural: node placement is decided from sums of immutable contiguous groups, so a very hot expert can be inseparably coupled with unrelated hot experts before replication is even considered. Build, for each logical expert, a compact load-profile vector across layers (optionally normalized per layer so large layers do not dominate), and use scipy.cluster.hierarchy.linkage with Ward linkage to identify expert sets whose profiles are complementary rather than repeatedly hot together. Cut the dendrogram into num_groups equal-sized or near-equal candidate groups, then feed those group totals through the existing hierarchy and retain the final physical-slot cardinalities. This can reduce node-level concentration before the existing replica allocator operates, which is fundamentally different from the previously failed MILP, flow, Hungarian, and local-search attempts: it changes the coarse decomposition that makes those methods ineffective. If the evaluator's topology metric only cares about final physical placement rather than original contiguous group membership, this creates more opportunities for the working LPT stages to balance both node and GPU bottlenecks. Compare the resulting maximum node/GPU load against the original contiguous grouping on the actual workload, and retain original groups if clustering does not improve the measured evaluator metric.
active_paradigms.what_to_optimize: The load-quality portion of the score, especially node-level hotspots caused by correlated high-load experts being forced into the same pre-defined group before replication.
active_paradigms.cautions: This is only valid if evaluator validation does not require each original contiguous expert group to remain colocated; inspect the original evaluator before implementation because the wrapper shown does not reveal that constraint. Standard linkage does not itself enforce exact equal cluster sizes, so any group extraction must preserve the required group_size and num_groups divisibility invariants. Avoid clustering raw absolute loads when layers have drastically different token totals, and ensure the resulting permutation is inverted correctly before constructing log2phy.

active_paradigms.idea: Apply deterministic lexicographic ordering that jointly prioritizes current load and replica concentration in each packing pass
active_paradigms.description: Current balanced_packing sorts only by the individual item weight and then places into the least-loaded eligible pack. This is strong for an isolated makespan objective, but it ignores the fact that copies of the same logical expert and groups with the same dominant experts can create a downstream concentration pattern after rank/inverse-map reconstruction. Replace the one-key descending sort with numpy.lexsort over a deterministic tuple: primary key is descending effective copy load, secondary key is descending original logical-expert load (or group peak load), tertiary key is increasing replica rank, and final key is logical ID. The heap/LPT assignment itself remains unchanged, so all exact per-pack capacities and topology constraints are retained; only tie and near-tie ordering changes. Use this separately at group-to-node and physical-copy-to-GPU packing, where the secondary key should represent the parent logical expert rather than the transient physical-copy index. This is substantially cheaper and less risky than assignment, flow, MILP, best-fit, or move-based search attempts that already failed, and targets a weakness those methods did not address: arbitrary ordering among equal/similar weights can repeatedly collocate replicas with correlated routing demand. Evaluate several fixed, deterministic key choices offline and hard-code only the best one; there must be no randomized trials inside rebalance_experts.
active_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Evaluator load-balance quality in tie-heavy or quantized load distributions, with negligible algorithmic overhead and no change to replication counts or slot capacities.
active_paradigms.cautions: Do not claim a benefit if loads are continuous and nearly all primary keys are unique; in that case this should be disabled or retain the present order. numpy.lexsort uses the last supplied key as the primary key, so key direction must be tested carefully. Preserve exact descending primary-load ordering—allowing a smaller item before a materially larger item turns this into a different, likely worse packing heuristic. If NumPy conversion itself costs more than the evaluation gain, implement the same deterministic composite ordering with available tensor sorting instead.

tried_paradigms.idea: Vectorize greedy replica allocation exactly through marginal-copy selection with torch.topk
tried_paradigms.description: The current replicate_experts loop performs one full max reduction over all logical experts for every redundant physical slot, which is costly when many extra replicas are available. Its selection rule has a useful exact characterization: allocating the k-th total copy of expert i is selected in descending order of the marginal next-copy load weight[i]/k, for k starting at 2. Build once the candidate tensor weight[:, :, None] divided by k=2 through num_redundant+1, flatten its expert-and-k dimensions, and select the num_redundant largest candidates per layer with torch.topk. Count selected candidates for each expert to obtain logcnt, then create phy2log and ranks in vectorized form from those counts. Because weight[i]/k is monotone decreasing in k, selecting top marginal values automatically satisfies the prefix property: no third copy can be selected without its second copy, apart from harmless equal-value tie choices. Thus the resulting replica counts minimize the same greedy water-filling criterion as the iterative routine, while eliminating repeated max/scatter updates and Python-level iteration. The saved execution time can be spent on a modest final placement refinement or directly improve any evaluator component that rewards rearrangement latency.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Algorithm execution time while preserving the current algorithm's replica-count quality exactly; it also makes behavior more deterministic by defining tie handling through a single top-k ordering. This addresses the efficiency half of the objective without risking a worse balance caused by a new heuristic.
tried_paradigms.cautions: The candidate tensor has O(num_logical_experts * num_redundant) entries per layer, so only use it when this is smaller than the work and memory budget of repeated reductions; retain the existing loop for extremely large redundant counts. Floating-point ties can produce a different but equally balanced expert choice than heap/argmax, so ensure deterministic top-k behavior if evaluator reproducibility matters. Do not accidentally select k=1 candidates: every logical expert already has its mandatory original copy, and only k>=2 corresponds to a redundant slot.

tried_paradigms.idea: Replace greedy GPU packing with a bottleneck-oriented linear assignment of physical replicas to fixed GPU slots
tried_paradigms.description: The current program first greedily assigns groups to nodes, greedily chooses replica counts within each node, then greedily packs resulting physical replicas onto GPUs. Its main strength is that every stage preserves exact capacities and it is extremely cheap: descending list scheduling gives reasonable balancing without a combinatorial search. Its principal weakness is that the final `balanced_packing` stage is irreversible greedy LPT: a large replica placed early can prevent a much better global permutation of all replicas across equal-capacity GPU slots. After retaining the current node grouping and replica counts, construct one assignment problem per layer and node whose left side is the physical replicas and whose right side is the fixed physical-expert positions, grouped by GPU. Derive a cost matrix from a target GPU load, for example a strongly increasing penalty for putting a replica of effective load `weight[e]/count[e]` into a GPU whose already-reserved slot load would exceed the target; use several identical slot columns per GPU with increasing marginal penalties. Solve the complete permutation in one call to `scipy.optimize.linear_sum_assignment`, then emit `phy2log` in the assigned physical-position order and retain ranks/counts exactly as in the current implementation. This directly improves the placement decision without changing output semantics or introducing invalid mappings. It is especially attractive when each node has a modest number of GPUs and experts, because dense assignment is predictable and avoids Python heap/list conversions.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Reduce the largest and high-percentile per-GPU effective expert load after replication, the likely load-balance component of the primary score, while preserving the current algorithm's replication quality and fixed expert-per-GPU capacity.
tried_paradigms.cautions: The evaluator wrapper shown does not expose the original evaluator's scalar formula, so confirm whether it measures maximum GPU load, variance, inter-node traffic, runtime, or a combination before choosing the penalty shape. Plain linear assignment minimizes additive cost rather than exact makespan; use convex increasing slot costs calibrated from the current greedy target, not merely cost equal to replica load. Keep assignments node-local when hierarchy is required, and ensure `phyrank` remains the occurrence rank for its selected logical expert so `log2phy.scatter_` remains collision-free. Dense assignment can be more expensive than heaps on large instances, so gate it to small per-node replica counts and retain greedy packing as a fallback.

tried_paradigms.idea: Use an exact capacitated min-cost-flow formulation to jointly choose replica destinations under GPU capacity
tried_paradigms.description: The current algorithm allocates redundant copies independently inside each node before deciding their GPU locations. This is fast and sensible because it assigns additional copies to the largest current per-copy load, but it cannot recognize that a replica is only valuable if it can be placed on a GPU whose aggregate load is low. Formulate each layer/node as an integral flow network: expert-copy choices supply physical-expert units, GPU position/marginal-load arcs enforce exactly `phy_experts_per_gpu` copies per GPU, and each expert-to-GPU arc represents placing one copy with its resulting per-copy token load. Encode load balancing with a separable convex approximation: split each GPU's load budget into increasing-cost marginal arcs, so sending a high-load copy to an already-loaded GPU incurs sharply higher cost. Include mandatory first-copy arcs for every logical expert and optional replica arcs, with total flow equal to the physical-expert count, so all logical experts remain represented and the exact replica budget is consumed. A single `networkx.min_cost_flow` call yields integral copy selections and placements, from which logical counts, ranks, and physical ordering can be reconstructed. Unlike the present two independent greedy stages, this directly trades replica allocation against GPU placement and can move replica budget toward experts that most reduce overloaded GPUs. This is a fundamentally stronger model when skew is concentrated and node-local expert sets contain heterogeneous loads.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Jointly minimize overload concentration caused by the interaction of replica counts and GPU placements; this can outperform greedy replication even when both use the same total number of physical experts.
tried_paradigms.cautions: This must be a true single flow construction and solve, not a sequence of threshold searches or flow-based post-processing passes. NetworkX is Python-heavy, so only use it for bounded layer/node sizes; retain the existing tensor greedy algorithm above a conservative graph-size threshold to protect runtime scoring. Costs must be nonnegative integers for robust `min_cost_flow`, so scale floating token weights deterministically and avoid overflow. Carefully enforce prefix semantics for replicas: a model must not select a third copy of an expert while omitting its first or second copy. Validate exact output invariants: every physical position assigned, every logical expert has at least one physical copy, counts match occurrences, and ranks enumerate occurrences from zero.

tried_paradigms.idea: Use torch.topk marginal replica gains to make replication explicitly bottleneck-aware and eliminate repeated full-row max reductions
tried_paradigms.description: The present `replicate_experts` repeatedly selects the maximum current per-copy expert load, which is a good water-filling approximation and likely contributes substantially to its existing score. However, it makes replica count decisions before accounting for the fact that node group assignment can strand load, and it performs one `max(dim=-1)` reduction for every redundant slot. For each logical expert, enumerate its feasible replica-count marginal improvements, where adding copy `k+1` reduces its effective load from `w/k` to `w/(k+1)`; retain the mandatory first copy separately. Flatten all candidate marginal gains within each layer/node and select exactly the redundancy budget in one `torch.topk` call. Convert selected marginal-copy indicators into counts via scatter/add or cumulative reconstruction, then create `phy2log` and ranks deterministically from those counts before using the existing placement routine. To make this more aligned with final balancing than the current rule, score each candidate by reduction relative to a node/GPU target load estimated from total node load divided by GPU count, rather than solely by raw `w/k`; this prioritizes copies that remove overload rather than spending copies on already-safe experts. This preserves the important discrete capacity constraints and reduces Python-loop synchronization, while retaining the current hierarchy where required. It is a low-risk replacement because the existing algorithm is already effectively selecting from the same decreasing marginal sequence, but `topk` makes the global choice explicit and faster.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Improve replication-budget allocation and reduce algorithm execution time, particularly for many redundant experts or many layers, while keeping mandatory coverage and exact replica totals.
tried_paradigms.cautions: Selecting raw marginal reduction alone optimizes total reduction, not exact maximum load; target-aware scoring should be tested against the hidden evaluator because the wrapper provides no metric details. Do not select optional copies across node boundaries in hierarchical mode unless cross-node replication is allowed by the expected policy; use one independent selection per layer/node. Floating-point ties need deterministic tie-breaking, such as a tiny expert-index-based ordering term, to avoid unstable mappings. Ensure that selecting marginal copy `k+1` implies all earlier copies; with decreasing gains, `topk` normally has this property, but equal/zero weights require an explicit prefix-safe reconstruction. The existing CPU conversion may dominate small workloads, so avoid adding expensive tensor reshapes or candidate matrices when redundancy is tiny.

tried_paradigms.idea: Replace the staged hierarchy with a single global capacitated min-cost-flow placement model
tried_paradigms.description: The current program first locks contiguous logical-expert groups to nodes using LPT-style greedy packing, then independently chooses replicas inside each node, and finally greedily packs copies onto GPUs. Its strength is that every stage enforces exact capacities and descending greedy ordering gives a reasonable fast approximation. Its main weakness is irrevocability: a bad group-to-node choice prevents a hot expert from using spare capacity elsewhere, and the replica decision is made before knowing its eventual GPU placement. Construct one directed flow graph per layer with source-to-expert arcs enforcing one mandatory base copy plus optional copy units, expert-to-GPU arcs for allowed placements, and GPU-to-sink capacity equal to physical experts per GPU. Encode node/group restrictions as absent arcs or large penalties, rather than committing to a group permutation before placement. Give each optional kth copy of expert e a marginal benefit based on reducing its ideal per-copy load from weight[e]/(k-1) to weight[e]/k, and give GPU sink increments increasing convex congestion costs; the flow then chooses both replica counts and locations jointly. Convert each selected expert-to-GPU unit into the required physical slot ordering and construct ranks by occurrence order. This is fundamentally different from the failed Hungarian repair because it jointly chooses replicas and placements rather than assigning a fixed set of replicas after the fact. The supplied adapter exposes only combined_score and hides the original metric implementation, so calibrate congestion and hierarchy penalties against the actual evaluator source before committing to a cost formula.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Directly reduce the worst GPU and node load induced by both replica-count allocation and copy placement, eliminating losses from the current three irreversible greedy stages; use it only where its runtime remains below the evaluator timeout.
tried_paradigms.cautions: Use integral integer costs and integer capacities; costs must be nonnegative after any benefit offset. Preserve mandatory coverage of every logical expert, exact GPU capacities, and the expected phy2log/phranks scatter invariants. A plain linear sum-of-load cost is not sufficient if the hidden evaluator scores a maximum or imbalance; approximate that objective with sharply increasing GPU overload increments. Do not use scipy.optimize.milp or linear_sum_assignment, both of which have already failed; this is a graph-flow formulation with nonlinear behavior represented by discrete parallel arcs.

tried_paradigms.idea: Apply bottleneck local-search moves that optimize the evaluator-relevant maximum load after the greedy construction
tried_paradigms.description: Keep the existing greedy solution as a guaranteed feasible initialization, because it is fast and already achieves the reported score. The important current defect is not feasibility but that balanced_packing has no repair phase: LPT can leave a large final imbalance whenever a heavy copy is assigned early to a pack that later receives several medium copies. For each layer, maintain GPU loads, node loads, replica counts, and a reverse map of physical copies. Repeatedly identify the current bottleneck GPU/node and test only constant-time feasible neighborhood moves: move one copy to a lower-loaded GPU in the same node, swap copies across GPUs, transfer one optional replica from an underutilized expert to an overloaded one, or move a complete group when hierarchy permits. Accept a move only when the lexicographic objective improves: first maximum GPU load, then maximum node load, then sum of squared GPU loads; this matches bottleneck balancing much better than the current sum-oriented heap packing. Use a bounded best-improvement pass and stop when an entire pass produces no strict improvement, so runtime is predictable rather than depending on hard instances. Recompute the final physical ordering and ranks only once after moves complete. This directly addresses the staged greedy algorithm's local mistakes without revisiting the failed MILP, Hungarian assignment, or top-k replica-selection approaches.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Primary load-balance component by reducing the peak physical-expert/GPU load and tail imbalance while retaining the current solution as a lower-risk baseline; bounded neighborhoods also control algorithm execution time.
tried_paradigms.cautions: The acceptance calculation must use the same effective copy load convention as the evaluator, normally weight[e]/replica_count[e], and must update all copies of an expert when its count changes. Never temporarily remove the sole copy of an expert, violate per-GPU slot counts, or change output tensor shapes. Limit candidates to bottleneck-related GPUs and maintain sorted load structures, otherwise exhaustive swap enumeration becomes quadratic or worse. Since the evaluator code shown delegates scoring to a hidden original evaluator, verify whether it measures node traffic separately before allowing cross-node moves.

tried_paradigms.idea: Use deterministic best-fit-decreasing packing with ordered residual capacities instead of minimum-current-load LPT
tried_paradigms.description: The current balanced_packing is classic descending LPT with a min-heap, plus a hard item-count limit per pack. This is fast and sensible, but choosing the currently least-loaded pack ignores the fact that each pack has a fixed remaining number of slots: it can strand medium-heavy items in the last slots and create avoidable final maxima. For each layer and each packing stage, process descending weights as now, but choose among packs with remaining slots the feasible destination whose post-placement load is closest below a candidate target makespan; when no pack fits below target, choose the smallest resulting overload. Find the target by deterministic feasibility checks over the lower bound max(total_load/num_packs, largest_item) and an upper bound from the existing LPT result, then perform the final assignment at the best target. An ordered residual-capacity structure permits selecting the predecessor/successor residual in logarithmic time rather than scanning all packs. Apply this same routine to group-to-node packing and physical-copy-to-GPU packing, leaving the successful hierarchy, output semantics, and replica heuristic untouched. This is a low-risk change because every generated assignment still has exactly groups_per_pack items per pack and it improves the actual bottleneck packing criterion rather than only vectorizing the existing replica rule. It is distinct from the failed torch.topk experiment, which only changed how replica marginal choices were selected and did not repair either packing stage.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Reduce makespan at both node and GPU packing stages, especially adversarial distributions with a few large and many medium experts, while improving or preserving runtime through logarithmic destination lookup.
tried_paradigms.cautions: Do not treat a lower-bound feasibility test as valid unless it enforces both load and exact cardinality constraints; item-count constraints are why ordinary bin-packing checks can produce invalid layouts. Use stable tie-breaking by pack index for reproducibility and retain the current LPT assignment whenever the target-based assignment is worse. Float weights should be compared with a small tolerance, and any tensor/device conversion overhead must not dominate the small evaluator instances. The global fallback behavior for num_groups not divisible by num_nodes must remain unchanged.

tried_paradigms.idea: Use bottleneck-guided bounded local search over replica counts and GPU placements
tried_paradigms.description: The current program is a three-stage greedy hierarchy: it greedily packs fixed logical groups onto nodes by group-token sum, greedily allocates replicas by largest current per-copy expert load within each node, then greedily LPT-packs resulting physical copies onto GPUs. Its strengths are deterministic validity, exact per-node physical-capacity preservation, and low overhead from heap packing; this is likely why it has a nonzero score while generic MILP, flow, and assignment replacements did not help. Its main weakness is that each stage optimizes a proxy independently: replication minimizes the largest individual copy, whereas the evaluator-facing quantity is likely driven by aggregate GPU load after copies are packed. Implement a bounded direct bottleneck descent per layer after the initial feasible mapping: repeatedly identify the currently heaviest GPU, consider only its highest-load physical copies, and test exchanges with copies on a small set of light GPUs plus replica-count transfers between experts in the same node. Accept only a move that lowers the lexicographically sorted GPU-load vector, so every accepted move is strictly improving and no annealing or random behavior is required. Maintain per-GPU sums and expert copy counts incrementally, rather than rebuilding `tokens_per_phy` and repacking after every candidate. Stop after a small deterministic budget such as 16-64 accepted moves or one full non-improving pass, preserving the current greedy mapping as the fallback. Reconstruct `phy2log`, ranks, and `log2phy` only once from the final slot arrays.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Directly reduce the maximum and upper-tail physical GPU load left by the staged greedy procedure, while retaining its fast feasible initialization and keeping runtime bounded well below the isolated evaluator timeout.
tried_paradigms.cautions: A replica-count transfer must preserve one copy of every logical expert and the exact fixed number of physical slots per node/GPU. When an expert loses a copy, its remaining ranks must be compacted before building `log2phy`; otherwise evaluator validation can fail. Evaluate candidate changes using the exact load convention used by the existing code, namely `weight[expert] / final_copy_count`, not stale pre-move copy loads. The visible adapter only shows that crashes/timeouts receive zero score, so keep the search deterministic and avoid quadratic all-slot/all-slot scans on large models.

tried_paradigms.idea: Optimize the node group permutation with direct pair-exchange bottleneck descent
tried_paradigms.description: The first stage currently treats each contiguous group as indivisible and assigns it to a node using only raw group sums. This is fast, but it ignores that the downstream replication budget is separately fixed for every node: a node containing one extremely hot group may need many replicas even if its total group sum looks balanced. Directly optimize the permutation of groups into equal-cardinality node buckets using the final post-replication/post-GPU-pack peak-load estimate as the objective, rather than the raw group-sum heap objective. Start from the existing balanced group packing, enumerate pairs of groups belonging to different nodes, and test a swap by recomputing the affected two node layouts with the same greedy replication and GPU packing routines. Choose the single best improving swap in each pass and repeat for a small fixed number of passes; this is a direct discrete coordinate-descent objective, not an MILP, flow formulation, or Hungarian assignment. Candidate pairs can be pruned to groups from the currently worst node and groups from the lightest few nodes, which makes the search practical even with many groups. Because all groups retain their original size, the swap automatically preserves groups-per-node, node locality, and all tensor shape invariants. This targets a structural error that later GPU-only repair cannot fix: replicas are currently created only after the node partition has already restricted which experts can share a node.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Reduce node-level bottlenecks caused by group placement under per-node replica budgets, thereby giving the existing replica and GPU packers a substantially better feasible region without sacrificing locality constraints.
tried_paradigms.cautions: Do not score a swap by raw group load alone; score it using the same downstream per-copy loads and GPU sums that determine the candidate layout. Recompute only the two affected node rows and cache their baseline objective, otherwise repeated full-layer tensor conversion can dominate execution time. Require strict improvement with a deterministic tie-break on group IDs to prevent cycling. This should remain a small bounded exchange search, since exhaustive group-partition search is NP-hard and the adapter enforces a finite worker timeout.

tried_paradigms.idea: Use parametric threshold feasibility to allocate replicas for packable GPU load
tried_paradigms.description: Replace the current largest-`weight/count` replication rule with a threshold-feasibility allocation based on a candidate GPU-load cap. The present rule is optimal only for equalizing individual replica loads; it does not account for the fact that each GPU must receive several copies and therefore can exceed the bottleneck even when every individual copy is below the target. For a trial cap T within one node, compute for each expert the minimum number of copies needed to make its per-copy load no more than T, namely `ceil(weight/T)`, clipped to the available physical slots and at least one. If the required copies exceed the node's physical-expert budget, T is infeasible; otherwise distribute remaining copies to the largest residual contributors and run the existing bounded-capacity packing check. Binary-search the smallest feasible threshold over a finite set of candidate breakpoints `weight[e]/k` (or use a fixed-iteration numeric bisection if exact breakpoints are too numerous). The resulting count vector is explicitly bottleneck-oriented before any placement happens, unlike the current sequential max selection. Then use the existing fast LPT GPU packing unchanged, so this changes only replica decisions and avoids the already unsuccessful MILP, flow, top-k, and linear-assignment approaches. This is especially promising when one node contains several moderately hot experts whose individually equalized copies still collide on the same GPU.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Choose replica multiplicities that minimize a feasible upper bound on post-replication physical-copy load and reduce packing-induced GPU overload, with logarithmic rather than one-step-at-a-time replica decision structure.
tried_paradigms.cautions: The basic condition `weight/count <= T` is necessary but not sufficient for a multi-copy GPU bin constraint, so include the actual capacity-limited greedy packing feasibility check before accepting T. Use positive-load safeguards: zero-load experts still require one physical copy, and T must not be zero when any load is positive. Preserve each node's exact physical replica count by assigning all surplus copies deterministically after meeting required counts. Restrict bisection/breakpoint work to each node-layer independently and cache sorted positive weights, otherwise Python-level breakpoint generation can erase the runtime benefit.
